title: What are event bubbling, capturing, and delegation?
description: How events propagate through the DOM tree, phase control with addEventListener options, and delegation for dynamic content and fewer listeners.

data.text: **Question:** What are event bubbling, capturing, and delegation?

When you click a nested element, the DOM delivers the event in three phases: **capture** (root → target), **target**, then **bubble** (target → root). By default listeners fire in the bubble phase, which is what makes **event delegation** possible: instead of attaching a listener to every item, attach **one** listener to a common ancestor and use `event.target.closest(selector)` to identify which item fired. This cuts memory and setup cost on large lists, and it keeps working for elements **added later** — the listener was never on them in the first place.

**Propagation mechanics:**
- **Capture phase**: event travels window → document → … → parent of target. `addEventListener(type, fn, true)` or `{ capture: true }` subscribes here
- **Target phase**: the event reaches the target; both capture and bubble listeners at the target fire in registration order
- **Bubble phase**: event travels back up; default listeners (`{}` options) fire here. Not all events bubble (focus/blur don't — use focusin/focusout; mouseenter/leave don't bubble — but delegation still works because their non-bubbling siblings or capture do)
- `event.stopPropagation()` halts further propagation (up or down); `stopImmediatePropagation()` also stops other listeners on the same element

**Delegation pattern:**
- Listener on the container; `event.target` is the deepest element that fired; `event.target.closest('.row')` finds the ancestor row even if you clicked an icon inside it
- Works for content rendered after page load — lists, tables, nested widgets
- One listener vs thousands: noticeable for 10k-row tables and repeated re-renders
- Enables automatic handling of dynamic content without re-attaching handlers

**Trade-offs and pitfalls:**
- Memory per listener is small, but setup cost and retained closures aren't — delegation wins at scale
- `closest` from target can escape the delegated container if markup nests unexpectedly — check `container.contains(el)`
- Stopping propagation must be deliberate: a child that calls stopPropagation silently disables ancestor delegation
- Some behaviors need per-element listeners (drag sources with DataTransfer state, hover CSS-driven UI) — delegate what bubbles, don't force it
- Frameworks already delegate: React attaches at the root and simulates bubbling through its synthetic event system — knowing the DOM mechanism explains React's event quirks

data.title: Per-row listeners vs one delegated listener
Delegation explains React events
data.text: React attaches a single listener to the app root and dispatches synthetic events through its own component tree — that's DOM delegation at framework scale. It's why event handlers 'keep working' for re-rendered children and why stopping propagation in React must use e.stopPropagation() in the synthetic event, not the native one.

Interviewers want to assess:
- The three-phase model and that default listeners are bubble-phase
- The closest() delegation pattern and why it handles dynamic content
- Knowledge of non-bubbling events and their bubbling alternatives
- Awareness of when delegation is inappropriate

items: Using event.target instead of closest — clicking an icon inside a row selects the icon, not the row
Forgetting that stopPropagation in a child kills ancestor delegation
Delegating mouseenter/mouseleave — they don't bubble; use mouseover/mouseout or capture
Not checking container.contains(el) — closest can find an ancestor outside the delegated list
Re-attaching delegated listeners on every render instead of once
Delegating single-item UI (a hero button) — no scale benefit, added indirection
How do capture-phase listeners let you intercept events before a child's handler?
Why do focus and mouseenter not bubble, and what do you use for delegation instead?
How does React's synthetic event delegation differ from raw DOM delegation?
When would you still attach per-element listeners?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Events flow capture → target → bubble; default listeners fire while bubbling
Delegation: one ancestor listener + event.target.closest() — fast, dynamic-safe
Non-bubbling events (focus, mouseenter) need variants for delegation
stopPropagation in children can silently disable delegated handlers
data.takeaway: Let the event come to you: one listener on a stable ancestor handles every current and future child, and closest() tells you exactly which one was clicked.
